title: The German Sentence
desc: One word is missing from a German sentence: an article in its case, an adjective with its ending, a verb in its person, a past form, or a word in its place in the order of the sentence. The word is chosen from tiles at the first levels and written at the higher ones.

intro.h: The article. The article shows the gender, the number, and the case of its noun.
eg: der Mann, den Mann, dem Mann, des Mannes; ein Pferd, einen Mann, einem Freund

intro.h: The adjective. After der, die, or das the adjective takes a weak ending; after ein, or with no article, it shows the gender and the case itself. After sein it takes no ending.
eg: der gute Mann, ein guter Mann, guter Wein; der König ist gut

intro.h: Person. The ending of the verb shows the person and the number of its subject, and some strong verbs change their vowel in the second and third persons singular.
eg: ich spreche, du sprichst, er spricht

intro.h: The past. The Perfekt is haben or sein with the past participle; verbs of motion or change of state take sein.
eg: er hat das Bett gemacht; sie ist gekommen

intro.h: The order of words. In a main clause the finite verb stands second, and a participle, an infinitive, or a separable prefix goes to the end. In a clause after dass or weil the finite verb goes to the end.
eg: heute gibt der König der Frau ein Buch; der Zug kommt um acht an; dass er heute kommt

items.why: Mann is the object of sieht, so it is in the accusative, and the masculine accusative is den.

items.en: The woman gives the king a book.
items.fr: Die Frau gibt ______ König ein Buch.
items.why: The one who receives is in the dative, and the masculine dative is dem.
Pferd is neuter, and the neuter nominative of the article is das.
Pferd is neuter and the object, and the neuter accusative of the indefinite article is ein.
Mann is masculine and the object, so the indefinite article is einen.
Mit takes the dative, and the masculine dative of the indefinite article is einem.
The possessor is in the genitive, and the feminine genitive of the article is der.
Stadt is feminine and the object, and the feminine accusative is die.
After der the adjective in the nominative singular takes the weak ending -e.
After ein the adjective shows the gender itself, so the masculine nominative is guter.
After den the adjective takes -en.
Without an article the adjective takes the strong ending, and the dative plural is -en: mit guten Freunden.
After ein the neuter adjective shows the gender itself: ein kleines Haus.
Without an article the adjective takes the strong ending, and the masculine nominative is -er.
After die in the plural the adjective takes -en.
An adjective that is the predicate, after sein, takes no ending.
Ich takes the ending -e, without the change of vowel: ich spreche.
Du takes -st, and sprechen changes e to i: du sprichst.
Er takes -t, and geben changes e to i: er gibt.
The first person plural of sein is sind.
The second person plural of haben is habt.
The third person singular of werden is wird.
Sie, they, is the third person plural, and its verb ends in -en.
The second person singular of sein is bist.
Machen forms the Perfekt with haben, and er takes hat.
Kommen is a verb of motion and forms the Perfekt with sein: sie ist gekommen.
The past participle of sprechen is gesprochen, and it stands at the end.
The past participle of sehen is gesehen.
The full verb werden has the participle geworden. Worden is used only in the passive.
The past participle of geben is gegeben.
The Präteritum of sein in the first person singular is war. Wäre is the Konjunktiv II.
The Präteritum of haben is hatte. Hätte is the Konjunktiv II.

items.en: Today the king gives the woman a book.
items.fr: Heute ______ König der Frau ein Buch.
items.why: In a main clause the finite verb stands second. Heute fills the first place, so the verb comes next and the subject follows it: heute gibt der König.

items.en: I know that the king gives the woman a book.
items.why: After dass the finite verb goes to the end of the clause.

items.en: The king has given the woman a book.
items.fr: Der König hat der Frau ein Buch ______.
items.why: The past participle goes to the end of the clause, and hat stands second.

items.en: Does the king give the woman a book?
items.fr: ______ der König der Frau ein Buch?
items.why: A question without a question word puts the finite verb first, and der König takes gibt.
Ankommen has a separable prefix, and in a main clause the prefix goes to the end: der Zug kommt um acht an.

items.en: He wants to read the book.
items.why: After a modal verb the infinitive goes to the end without zu.

items.en: Because the king is ill, he stays at home.
items.fr: Weil der König krank ist, ______ er zu Hause.
items.why: The subordinate clause fills the first place, so the verb of the main clause follows at once: bleibt er.

items.en: I believe that he is coming today.
items.why: After dass the verb goes to the end, and er takes kommt.
